extracted.intended_audience: Citizens of New York / the American public interested in constitutional design (readers of The Federalist)
extracted.subtask_description: An 18th-century political essay (Federalist Nos. 54–56) arguing standards for apportioning representatives among States, the proper size and term of the House, and the qualifications/knowledge and safeguards appropriate for federal representatives. Focuses on representation, census rules (including the slave question), and institutional safeguards against corruption and ill-effect of small/large assemblies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge and acquirements required of a federal representative
rubrics_metrics.description: Representatives must acquire extensive information: local/state internal circumstances, commerce regulations, treaties, the commercial policy and laws of other nations, and some knowledge of the law of nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text: 'A branch of knowledge which belongs to the acquirements of a federal representative ... is that of foreign affairs. In regulating our own commerce he ought to be not only acquainted with the treaties between the United States and other nations, but also with the commercial policy and laws of other nations. He ought not to be altogether ignorant of the law of nations.' Some of this knowledge can be acquired privately, but much must come from public sources and practical attention during legislative service. Local/state codes and experience in state legislatures will aid representatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length and frequency of elections — biennial terms preferred
rubrics_metrics.description: Biennial (two-year) elections are justified as being 'as useful to the affairs of the public' and 'safe to the liberty of the people.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments given: longer term allows representatives to acquire necessary information, reduces burdens from travel and arrangements for distant members, decreases the attractiveness of spurious/unlawful elections (since annulment takes time), and provides continuity and experience. Annual elections would exacerbate investigation/deters annulment issues and encourage illicit returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apportionment standard: population as measure for representation (same rule for direct taxes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of people in each State ought to be the standard for regulating the proportion of representatives; the same rule is to be used for direct taxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay distinguishes that while numbers are the natural scale for representation (personal rights), taxation relates to property and wealth (an imperfect measure). Nevertheless the convention adopted population as the practicable rule for both apportionment and taxation because it had general sanction and was the least objectionable practicable rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of slaves in the census (three-fifths compromise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Slaves are to be regarded in the 'mixed character of persons and of property'—the Constitution's compromise treats them as inhabitants but 'divested of two fifths of the man' (i.e., three-fifths rule).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay defends compromise by noting slaves are in some respects persons (protected in life/limb, punishable) and in others property (vendible, compelled labor), so counting them partly in representation and taxation follows the laws under which they live. It also argues political practicability: if slaves were fully excluded or fully included, Southern States would resist or be unjustly disadvantaged; the compromise secures mutual moderation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation should reflect both persons and property (some regard to wealth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Representation should consider protection of property as well as persons; some attention ought to be paid to property in the choice of representatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning: government exists to protect property as well as persons; states' relative wealth should give them some proportional influence because unlike wealthy individuals within a State, a rich State cannot influence other States' choices. Thus a superior share of representation can secure advantages legitimately owed to more opulent States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the same census rule for representation and taxation to balance incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Extending the same rule to both representation and taxation prevents States from having unilateral incentives to misreport population (inflate for representation, reduce for taxation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay: by making the census determine both representation and direct taxes, the opposing interests will 'control and balance each other' producing greater impartiality and discouraging exaggeration or understatement of inhabitants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate total number of representatives: neither too few nor too many
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be a certain minimum number necessary 'to secure the benefits of free consultation and discussion, and to guard against too easy a combination for improper purposes,' but the number must not be so large as to produce confusion, intemperance, or mob tendencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical projections: initial number 65, with census-based increases (one per 30,000). Numbers should grow over time (100, 200, 400 estimated) to alleviate fears about smallness. The text warns against arithmetical extrapolation (proportion rules across very large/small polities may mislead) and notes extremes (too few yields risk of combination; too many yields mob rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal legislative business requires broader information and justifies longer terms and different composition than State legislatures
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal legislation is more novel and difficult than State legislative business and thus calls for longer terms, more time to form a federal code, and representatives who can acquire larger-scale knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay emphasizes the laborious task of inaugurating government and forming federal codes; improvements become easier with time and past transactions provide sources for new members. Because federal acts take effect without individual States' intervention, representatives must have broader and deeper information than state legislators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical sources of federal representatives' information: state laws and service in state legislatures
rubrics_metrics.description: State codes and prior service in state legislatures supply much of the local information required for federal legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: representatives will often have been members of their State legislatures, and state laws/proceedings contain preparatory labor and local information which can shorten federal legislative work. A skillful individual with access to state codes might compile federal laws on many internal subjects without extensive oral information.

rubrics_metrics.name: House authority over elections and the timing problem for annulling spurious elections
rubrics_metrics.description: Each House must judge the elections, qualifications, and returns of its members; with very frequent elections a long process of investigating and annulling spurious returns can render redress ineffective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because a portion of a year would unavoidably elapse in disputed cases, annual elections would make it feasible for illegitimate members to hold seats long enough to serve their purposes, creating a perverse encouragement of unlawful means to obtain returns. Longer terms reduce this incentive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safeguards against corruption via ineligibility to civil office and limited emoluments
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of Congress are rendered ineligible to civil offices that may be created or have increased emoluments during their term, limiting the President/Senate's ability to 'buy' fidelity by appointments; emoluments of office are otherwise insufficient to corrupt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues it's improbable foreign gold or appointment power (given restrictions) could subvert the federal government; combined with state oversight and accountability to the people, these institutional constraints reduce risk of mercenary combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of geography and travel burdens in term length
rubrics_metrics.description: Distance and travel arrangements for representatives make longer (two-year) terms less burdensome and thus more attractive to fit men than annual terms would be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay notes that travel burdens could be a 'serious objection with fit men' if service were limited to one year but are much mitigated by two-year terms. This practical consideration supports longer terms for federal representatives.
